::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 10) you can:

1. **extend** message passing to typed nodes and edges, and hand-simulate one R-GCN layer on a small typed graph;
2. **derive** R-GCN's parameter explosion and both repairs — basis and block-diagonal decompositions — with exact counts;
3. **describe** attention-based heterogeneous models (HAN's metapaths, HGT's typed attention) at architecture level and choose between them for a stated schema;
4. **assemble** encoder–decoder KG completion (R-GCN encoder + DistMult decoder) and compare it against Week 4's shallow embeddings honestly — same decoder, same eval;
5. **map** a relational database schema onto a heterogeneous graph — the bridge Week 14 will drive a truck over.
:::

## The last untyped week

Week 9 ended by naming the assumption every graph in this course's GNN arc has
shared: *every edge meant the same thing.* Cora's edges were all citation. The
karate club's were all friendship. The barbell's were all wire. One adjacency
matrix, one aggregation, one learned way of listening — a simplification so
comfortable it stopped feeling like one.

Now look at the graphs from the *other* half of this course. In
[Week 4](04-knowledge-graphs.qmd), *located_in* and *treats* and *capital_of*
were so unalike that each got its own geometric personality — translations,
rotations, diagonal scalings — and we abandoned message passing entirely,
scoring triples straight out of a lookup table. For six weeks the two threads
of this course have run in parallel: knowledge graphs with rich types and no
message passing; message passing with rich learning and no types. This week
they merge, and the merge is not a formality — it forces two genuinely new
problems and one uncomfortable measurement.

The first problem is architectural: what does "aggregate the neighborhood" even
mean when the neighborhood contains an author, three citations, and a venue?
The answer — give every relation its own transformation — takes one line to
say and, on a real knowledge graph, immediately writes a bill for **4.75
million parameters per layer**. You will compute that bill exactly, and the
two classic ways of talking it down. The second problem is subtler: when
neighborhoods speak through *typed multi-hop patterns* (co-authorship is
author–paper–author, not any single edge), who decides which patterns matter?
Two architectures answer differently — one asks a human, one learns it — and
choosing between them is a real engineering decision you will practice.

And the uncomfortable measurement: once an R-GCN can *encode* entities of a
knowledge graph, the obvious move is to bolt Week 4's DistMult decoder on top
and declare the lookup table obsolete. We ran that experiment — same data,
same loss, same filtered evaluation as Lab 4, everything matched — and the
lookup table won. Holding the theorem-grade elegance of typed message passing
in one hand and that table in the other, without dropping either, is this
week's version of the discipline this course keeps preaching: architectures
are hypotheses, and the benchmark does not care how pretty they are.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** DBLP is a real academic graph: 4,057 authors,
14,328 papers, 7,723 terms, 20 conferences, with typed edges for writing,
mentioning, and publishing. The task: classify authors into four research
areas. An MLP on author features alone — no graph at all — scores 79.0%.
Predict the accuracy of a two-layer *typed* message-passing network that also
reads papers, terms, and venues. And predict what an *untyped* GNN (all edges
merged into one soup) would do to that number.

::: {.predict-answer}
Measured, three seeds: the typed network reaches **84.0 ± 0.7** — five points
over features-alone, earned mostly through author–paper–author co-authorship
signal that the MLP cannot see. The untyped soup is the interesting control:
merging edge types forces one shared weight onto co-authorship, term
co-occurrence, and venue links simultaneously, and the benchmark literature's
answer (you will meet the HGB paper below) is that it costs real accuracy —
though less than the architecture papers implied, a nuance this lecture takes
seriously in §6.
:::
:::

## The object: schemas, instances, and what projections destroy

This week's central object deserves the course's formal treatment, because
everything downstream is parameterized by it.

::: {#def-w10-hetero .definition name="Heterogeneous graph and schema"}
A **heterogeneous graph** is a graph plus a type system: a set of node types
$\mathcal{A}$, a set of relation types $\mathcal{R}$, a type assigned to every
node and every edge, and a **schema** — a small meta-graph over the types
saying which may connect through which relations. Keep schema and instance
sharply distinct when reading: the schema is the data model (a handful of
types), the instance is its population (thousands of nodes) — and every
architecture this week is parameterized by the *schema* while computing on
the *instance*.
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w10-hetero.html >}}

The five-node instance on the right is this week's karate club — small enough
to hand-compute, rich enough to break untyped intuitions — and its scalar
features are chosen so you can follow every number.

The real dataset behind this week's measurements deserves the same anatomical
attention, because its quirks are every heterogeneous dataset's quirks. DBLP,
as packaged for hetero-GNN research: **4,057 authors** (the nodes we classify,
into four research areas), **14,328 papers**, **7,723 terms**, **20
conferences**; edge types `writes`, `mentions`, `published_in`, each stored
in both directions.

Now the quirks. Feature dimensions differ *per type* —
authors carry 334-dimensional bags of words, papers 4,231, terms 50 — so no
single weight matrix can even accept "the neighbors" as one batch; typed
models are forced on you by linear algebra before any accuracy argument.
Conference nodes ship with *no features at all* — twenty nodes, pure
identity — and the standard fix (give them a constant scalar and let their
embedding be entirely relational) is a tiny preview of the featureless-entity
problem that dominates the KG half of this lecture. And the labels live on
only one type: authors. The task is not "classify the graph"; it is "classify
one type, using all of them" — which is exactly the shape of most industrial
problems (classify the *customers*, using orders, products, sessions).

This shape is everywhere once you look. OGB's academic benchmark
(MAG; [Hu et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00687)) is
authors–papers–institutions–fields at two million nodes. Biomedical graphs
tie drugs, proteins, diseases, side-effects into typed multigraphs
(Week 5's toy KG, industrialized). E-commerce is users–items–sessions–
queries. In each, the types are not annotation on top of the data — they
*are* the data model, and flattening them is a modeling decision someone
should have to defend in review.

You have, in fact, been here before, in the smallest possible dose: the
bipartite graphs of [Week 1](01-why-graphs.qmd) — users and movies, two
node types, one relation — are the minimal heterogeneous graph, and the
recommendation systems built on them were heterogeneous modeling before
the word arrived. This week's apparatus is that idea with the training
wheels off: many types, many relations, and a schema instead of a
two-column convention.

Why not simplify? The standard temptation, which whole applied literatures
indulged for years, is to *project*: co-authorship networks are
author–paper–author collapsed to author–author; protein networks collapse
drug–protein–disease tripartite structure to protein–protein. Projection is
lossy in ways you can now name precisely. It forgets multiplicity (two shared
papers or ten — one edge either way), forgets the mediator's identity (shared
*NeurIPS* paper or shared workshop note), and forgets every path that mixes
relations. [Week 1](01-why-graphs.qmd) called choosing a representation the
first modeling decision; the heterogeneous graph is the representation that
declines to decide prematurely — it keeps the types and lets the *model*
learn what to collapse. The price is that the model must now be told how to
read types, which is the rest of this lecture.

## R-GCN: one weight matrix per relation

The R-GCN update ([Schlichtkrull et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06103),
your required reading) is [Week 7's template](07-gnn-design.qmd) with the
aggregation slot split by relation:

$$
h_v' \;=\; \sigma\Big(\, W_0\, h_v \;+\; \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}}\ \sum_{u \in N_r(v)} \frac{1}{c_{v,r}}\, W_r\, h_u \Big)
$$ {#eq-w10-rgcn}

where —

- $h_v$ is node $v$'s current representation and $h_v'$ its post-update one
  (the prime always means "after this layer");
- $\sigma$ is a pointwise nonlinearity (ReLU here, in the paper, and in Lab 10);
- $W_0$ is the self-loop weight — the node listening to itself;
- $\mathcal{R}$ is the set of relation types, each direction counted separately;
- $N_r(v)$ is $v$'s neighborhood under relation $r$ alone, and $W_r$ is that
  relation's own transformation — the "typed" in typed message passing;
- $c_{v,r} = |N_r(v)|$ is the per-relation normalizer: the mean is taken
  *within* each channel, so three co-authors do not outvote one citation
  merely by count.

Three small-print items hide in @eq-w10-rgcn, each of which will bill you
later if skipped now. Each relation $r$ — *and each direction*: an incoming
`cites` is a different channel from an outgoing one, because being cited and
citing are different evidence about a paper (prominence versus topical
ancestry), so a graph with $R$ relations runs $2R$ typed channels plus the
self-loop $W_0$ — and that factor of two is about to matter enormously in the
parameter count. The normalizer averages within each relation — and the paper
also offers a learnable variant of $c$, an early whisper of §6's attention,
since "how loudly may this channel speak" is exactly the quantity attention
would make input-dependent. And aggregation
across relations is a plain **sum** — after Week 7 you can immediately ask
whether that slot could be attention instead; hold the question until §6,
where two architectures answer it.

Every symbol earns its keep in one worked update at paper $P_1$ of our toy —
features $h(A_1){=}1$, $h(A_2){=}2$, $h(P_1){=}1$, $h(P_2){=}3$, $h(V){=}2$,
scalar weights $W_0{=}1$, $W_{\text{writes}}{=}\tfrac12$,
$W_{\text{cites}}{=}1$, $W_{\text{pub}^{-1}}{=}\tfrac14$:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w10-rgcn.html >}}

Read the ledger the way the network does. The `writes` channel *averages* its
two authors ($\tfrac{1+2}{2} = 1.5$) before its weight touches them; the
citation, alone on its channel, arrives at full strength; the venue whispers
through a deliberately small weight. Total: $1 + 0.75 + 3 + 0.5 =
\mathbf{5.25}$. Now collapse the types — one shared weight, one plain mean
over all four neighbors — and watch what the collapse does:

$$
h'_{\text{untyped}}(P_1) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{1+2+3+2}{4} \;=\; \mathbf{2.00}
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad h'_{\text{typed}}(P_1) = \mathbf{5.25}
$$ {#eq-w10-collapse}

where — the leading $1$ is the self term ($W_0 h_{P_1} = 1 \cdot 1$), the
shared weight $W = \tfrac12$ replaces all three typed weights, and the mean
runs over all four neighbors $\{A_1, A_2, P_2, V\}$ regardless of relation.
The number matters less than what died on
the way to it: in the untyped layer there is *no parameter whose job is to say
citations matter more than venues*. Not "harder to learn" — nonexistent. Typed
weights are not a performance tweak; they are the difference between a
preference the optimizer can find and a preference the hypothesis class
cannot express.

The full procedure — @eq-w10-rgcn run at every node — is short enough to
state completely, and stating it pays: Lab 10's first exercise, `rgcn_update`,
implements it line for line.

::: {#alg-w10-rgcn .algorithm name="One R-GCN Layer"}
One pass of typed message passing: @eq-w10-rgcn computed for every node.

**Input:** features $h_u$ for all nodes; relation set $\mathcal{R}$ with
inverse channels included; weights $W_0, \{W_r\}_{r \in \mathcal{R}}$;
nonlinearity $\sigma$. **Output:** updated features $h_v'$ for all nodes.

1. **for** each node $v$ **do**
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$m \leftarrow W_0\, h_v$ (the self-channel)
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each relation $r \in \mathcal{R}$ **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**if** $N_r(v) = \varnothing$ **then** **continue**
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$m \leftarrow m + \frac{1}{|N_r(v)|} \sum_{u \in N_r(v)} W_r\, h_u$
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$h_v' \leftarrow \sigma(m)$
8. **end for**
9. **return** $\{h_v'\}$
:::

Line 5 is where the ledger lives — mean within the channel first, the
channel's weight second — and the cost is $O\big(\sum_r |E_r| \cdot d^2\big)$
per layer: every edge moved once through its relation's own $d \times d$
matrix ($|E_r|$ counts the edges of relation $r$, $d$ is the hidden width).
When parameters are basis-decomposed (§4, below), line 5 is unchanged except
that each $W_r$ is first assembled as $\sum_b a_{rb} V_b$. Lab 10's
`rgcn_update` is lines 1–9 with scalar weights and $\sigma$ set to the
identity; the DBLP model you will train is the same template with a learned
SAGE aggregator playing line 5 per edge type and the sum across relations
kept. Play the fader yourself:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w10-typed.html >}}

Two mechanical details separate people who have implemented this from people
who have read about it, and both are Lab 10 material. First, **inverse
channels are your job**. The equation's $N_r(v)$ quietly includes relations
like `cites⁻¹` — but PyG's `RGCNConv` knows nothing of inversion; it
propagates along the edges you give it, in the direction you give them. The
construction is three lines and absolutely load-bearing: concatenate the
edge list with its flipped copy, and give the flipped edges relation types
offset by $R$ (types $0..R{-}1$ forward, $R..2R{-}1$ inverse). Forget it and
a paper learns from what it cites but *nothing* from being cited — an
information diode nobody intended. More than one published "R-GCN
underperforms here" table owes part of its gap to this bug, which is why the
lab's assert makes you build the doubled list and checks the offsets
explicitly.

Second, **what is $h^{(0)}$ for a featureless entity?** FB15k-237
entities have no features — the input layer is an identity: each entity gets
a learnable row, i.e. the input to the first R-GCN layer *is* Week 4's lookup
table, and the encoder's claim is only ever that passing that table through
typed neighbors improves it. Keeping this straight is what makes the
showdown of §5 a controlled experiment rather than a vibe: both pipelines
start from the same object, and the encoder is exactly one added stage.

And to make the arithmetic muscle memory rather than a spectator sport, run
the same ledger at a second node yourself before the lab does it to you. At
$A_2$ (feature 2), only two channels speak — the self-loop and the inverse
channel `writes⁻¹` from the papers $A_2$ wrote:

$$
h'(A_2) \;=\; \underbrace{1 \cdot 2}_{\text{self}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{1 + 3}{2}}_{\texttt{writes}^{-1}\text{ from } \{P_1,\, P_2\}}
\;=\; 2 + 1 \;=\; \mathbf{3}
$$ {#eq-w10-selfcheck}

where — the self term is $W_0 = 1$ times $A_2$'s own feature $2$; the inverse
channel carries weight $\tfrac12$ and the mean of its papers' features
$\{1, 3\}$; no other channel touches an author in this instance. An author
is, to this layer, their own identity plus the average of what they write —
which reads like a job description because that is what typed aggregation
is, a learned job description per relation.

That is the whole architecture. On DBLP it is worth, as measured above, five
points over ignoring the graph — respectable, honest money. And the measured
five points come with a mechanism you can articulate: the MLP sees an
author's own words; two typed layers see the words of every co-authored
paper, every term those papers mention, and every venue that accepted them —
the co-authorship metapath assembled implicitly by stacking typed hops. The
trouble starts when you count what this machinery costs on a graph whose
$\mathcal{R}$ was not four but 237.

## The bill: $(2R{+}1) \cdot d^2$, and two ways to not pay it

Parameters per R-GCN layer follow from counting weight matrices — one per
typed channel, both directions, plus the self-loop:

$$
P_{\text{full}} \;=\; (2R + 1)\, d^2
\;\;\xrightarrow{\;R = 237,\ d = 100\;}\;\;
475 \times 10{,}000 \;=\; \mathbf{4{,}750{,}000}
$$ {#eq-w10-bill}

where —

- $R$ is the number of relation types; each runs two directed channels
  (hence $2R$), and the $+1$ is the self-loop;
- $d$ is the hidden width, so every weight matrix holds $d^2$ entries;
- the worked instance is FB15k-237's 237 relations at a modest $d = 100$ —
  per layer, before a single entity embedding.

Compare: the entire lookup table
of Week 4 was $14{,}541 \times 100 \approx 1.45$M. The encoder that was
supposed to enrich the embeddings costs three times the embeddings
themselves, per layer, and most of those matrices train on starvation
rations — FB15k-237's relation frequencies are wildly skewed, so rare
relations get full $d^2$ budgets and a few hundred triples of signal.
Overfitting is not a risk; it is the default.

Run the audit properly, because "wildly skewed" is a measurable, not an
adjective. FB15k-237 has 272,115 training triples over 237 relations — a
mean of ~1,148 per relation, but the distribution is the usual power law:
a handful of relations (`/people/person/profession`-style workhorses)
carry tens of thousands of triples while the long tail carries dozens. Now
put that against the budget: at $d = 100$, every relation's $W_r$ holds
10,000 free parameters *per direction*. A relation with 40 training triples
is being asked to estimate 20,000 numbers from 40 examples — a
parameters-per-example ratio of 500:1, which is not "prone to overfitting"
so much as *unspecified*: most of that matrix will be whatever the random
initialization and the regularizer left behind. The R-GCN paper knew it —
edge dropout and L2 are load-bearing in their recipe, not hygiene — but
regularization can only shrink the unspecified dimensions toward zero; it
cannot conjure signal. The decompositions attack the ratio itself.

Watch the basis count assemble, term by term, because each term is a design
decision. $B d^2$: the shared dictionary — thirty matrices that *all*
relations must express themselves through; this is where capacity lives,
and it no longer scales with $R$ at all. $2RB$: the per-relation mixing
coefficients — thirty numbers per channel, so our starving 40-triple
relation now estimates 30 numbers from 40 examples instead of 20,000; the
ratio just improved by three orders of magnitude. $d^2$: the self-loop,
which nobody decomposes because there is only one of it. Total at our
scale: $300{,}000 + 14{,}220 + 10{,}000 = 324{,}220$.

Both repairs from the R-GCN paper are one idea each, and you can hold them as
a pair of opposite bets:

::: {#def-w10-basis .definition name="Basis decomposition"}
Fix a budget of $B \ll 2R$ shared **basis matrices** $V_1, \dots, V_B$ and
express every relation's weight as a learned mixture,
$W_r = \sum_{b=1}^{B} a_{rb}\, V_b$, where $a_r \in \mathbb{R}^B$ is the
relation's coefficient vector. Read it as a bet that *relations are more
alike than they are numerous*: capacity lives in the shared dictionary,
per-relation identity in $B$ numbers per channel.
:::

The count drops accordingly — this is THE algebra of the week:

$$
P_{\text{basis}} \;=\;
\underbrace{B\, d^2}_{\text{shared bases}} \;+\;
\underbrace{2RB}_{\text{mixing coeffs.}} \;+\;
\underbrace{d^2}_{\text{self-loop}}
\;=\; 300{,}000 + 14{,}220 + 10{,}000 \;=\; \mathbf{324{,}220}
$$ {#eq-w10-basis}

where — $B = 30$ bases at FB15k-237's $R = 237$ and $d = 100$, the three
terms exactly as the previous paragraph assembled them: **14.7× fewer** than
@eq-w10-bill, with the per-relation identity carried entirely by the
length-30 coefficient
vector $a_r$. Stop on that object for a moment, because you have seen it
before: a small dense vector, one per relation, learned end-to-end, encoding
how the relation behaves — $a_r$ *is a relation embedding*, in precisely
[Week 4's](04-knowledge-graphs.qmd) sense, living inside the encoder's
weights instead of the decoder's score. (The optional CompGCN reading
([Vashishth et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03082)) makes
this bridge into a design principle: represent relations as vectors
outright and *compose* them with entity embeddings using operators lifted
from TransE and DistMult — the two halves of this course collapsing into one
equation.)

**Block-diagonal decomposition** bets the opposite: relations are
*independent*, but low-rank — each $W_r$ is a block-diagonal matrix of, say,
ten $\tfrac{d}{10} \times \tfrac{d}{10}$ blocks, so features interact only
within small sub-spaces. The count at our scale:

$$
P_{\text{block}} \;=\; 2R \cdot \tfrac{d^2}{10} \;+\; d^2
\;=\; 474{,}000 + 10{,}000 \;=\; \mathbf{484{,}000}
$$ {#eq-w10-blocks}

where — the $\tfrac{d^2}{10}$ per channel is the ten diagonal blocks' total
($10 \times (d/10)^2 = 1{,}000$ entries at $d = 100$), and the trailing
$d^2$ is, again, the undecomposed self-loop. Between the extremes, sharing
nothing across relations.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w10-params.html >}}

How do you choose $B$? Like every capacity knob: by validation, but with a
useful semantic reading attached. $B$ is a claim about how many *kinds of
relational behavior* exist in your schema — FB15k-237's 237 relations
plausibly cluster into far fewer behavioral families (part-whole relations,
professional relations, geographic containments…), and a trained model lets
you check: the coefficient vectors $a_r$ are inspectable, and relations
that share basis usage in $a_r$-space are relations the model considers
kin. That inspection is a legitimate deliverable — "the model discovered
that `capital_of` and `headquartered_in` load the same three bases" is an
interpretability artifact your Week-4 lookup decoder could never produce —
and it is an early ancestor of this line's current endpoint: the ULTRA
foundation model ([Galkin et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04562),
optional reading) drops the learned relation vocabulary
entirely and represents relations *by how they interact with each other*,
which is what lets one pretrained model answer queries on knowledge graphs
it has never seen. The basis trick, squinted at correctly, was the first
draft of relations-as-structure.

Which bet wins is an empirical question that depends on how much your
relations genuinely share, and the widget below is calibrated to give you the
engineering instinct: at $R \le 30$ the disease is mild and the full
treatment (which couples relations that may want independence) can cost more
than it saves; at $R = 237$ the full version is untrainable luggage and the
basis version is simply how the model ships.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w10-params.html >}}

<details>
<summary>Where R-GCN actually came from — one drawer of history</summary>
R-GCN was published at ESWC — the Extended *Semantic Web* Conference — not at
a machine-learning venue, and that address is the history in one line. The
Semantic Web community had spent fifteen years building typed graphs (RDF,
ontologies, SPARQL) and wanted statistical models; the statistical relational
learning community had spent the 2000s on Markov logic networks and lifted
inference; and the tensor-factorization line (RESCAL —
[Nickel et al., 2011](https://icml.cc/2011/papers/438_icmlpaper.pdf) — then
TransE — [Bordes et al., 2013](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2013/hash/1cecc7a77928ca8133fa24680a88d2f9-Abstract.html) —
and DistMult — [Yang et al., 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6575)) had
made KG completion a benchmark sport. R-GCN, with Kipf — of GCN fame
([Kipf & Welling, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907)) — among its
authors, was the moment the GCN wave broke over all
three: the paper is literally the GCN equation dressed for RDF, evaluated on
the SRL community's entity-classification datasets (AIFB, MUTAG, BGS, AM)
and the factorization community's FB15k-237. It won cleanly on the former —
typed features over typed structure is exactly its home game, and Lab 10
gives you AIFB for the same reason. On the latter it needed the DistMult
decoder to compete at all, which, as our measured showdown is about to say,
was foreshadowing.
</details>

## The showdown: learned encoder vs the lookup table

Assemble the pipeline the R-GCN paper proposed for link prediction. Week 4's
recipe was *lookup encoder* → DistMult score → margin loss → filtered
ranking. Keep every stage but the first: replace the lookup with entity
embeddings that a 1-layer R-GCN (basis, $B = 30$) has passed through the
graph, so every entity's vector now digests its typed neighborhood:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w10-encdec.html >}}

We ran the comparison with everything matched, and "matched" is a checklist,
not a mood — walk it, because designing this table *is* the lesson. Same
data: FB15k-237, the leak-audited split from Week 4. Same starting object:
learnable 100-dimensional entity vectors (the encoder passes them through
one basis-30 R-GCN layer with a residual; the lookup uses them raw). Same
decoder: DistMult, $\langle h, r, t\rangle$. Same loss: margin ranking
against one uniform corruption per positive — the exact recipe Lab 4
trained TransE with. Same evaluation: 2,000 sampled test facts, both
directions, filtered against all known triples, same sampling seed, so
every model answers the *same questions*. Same budget axis: 5 and 15
epochs, wall-clock recorded. What we did **not** match — and report instead
— is compute per epoch, because that asymmetry is not a confound, it is a
finding: one encoder epoch costs about 22 lookup epochs, and any deployment
decision has to price that in.

The whole protocol — the encoder–decoder template of
[Schlichtkrull et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06103) run under
Lab 4's rules — compresses to @alg-w10-showdown, and it is, line for line,
what Lab 10 has you run.

::: {#alg-w10-showdown .algorithm name="Encoder-Agnostic KG Completion Training"}
Trains and evaluates a KG-completion pipeline whose only free choice is the
encoder — identity lookup, or one R-GCN layer with a residual.

**Input:** training triples $T$; entity table $E \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$
($N$ entities, width $d$); relation table $R$ (one $d$-vector per relation);
encoder $\mathrm{enc}$; margin $\gamma$; epoch budget.
**Output:** trained $E, R$; filtered MRR and Hits@10.

1. **for** each epoch **do**
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each batch $B \subset T$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$Z \leftarrow \mathrm{enc}(E)$ — lookup: $Z = E$; R-GCN: one typed pass over *all* edges
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\tilde B \leftarrow$ corrupt one side of each triple uniformly
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\ell \leftarrow \mathrm{mean}\, \mathrm{ReLU}\big(\gamma - s(B) + s(\tilde B)\big)$, with $s(h,r,t) = \langle Z_h, R_r, Z_t \rangle$
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;take a gradient step on $\ell$
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
8. **end for**
9. **for** each sampled test fact, both directions **do**
10. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;score all candidates; set known-true answers (except the target) to $-\infty$
11. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;record the target's rank
12. **end for**
13. **return** mean reciprocal rank; fraction of ranks $\le 10$

:::

Line 3 is the entire cost asymmetry between the pipelines — the anatomy a
few paragraphs below prices it exactly. Line 5 is Lab 4's margin ranking
loss with DistMult's trilinear score, unchanged. Lines 9–13 are Week 4's
filtered ranking verbatim, so both pipelines answer the same 2,000 sampled
questions; Lab 10 hands you lines 1–8 as provided code and asks you to
write the referee, lines 9–13.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w10-showdown.html >}}

The lookup table wins every matched comparison on the board, and it does so
while spending **1/22nd** of the wall-clock. The trajectories carry more
information than the endpoints, so read them: from 5 to 15 epochs the
shallow DistMult moved 0.179 → 0.145 — *backwards* — and the encoder moved
0.126 → 0.122, a flat line bought for another sixteen minutes of GPU. The
first is honest-to-goodness overtraining: margin loss with unconstrained
embeddings keeps inflating norms after the ranking signal saturates, and
MRR pays for it (TransE dodges this with its unit-sphere renormalization —
Week 4's "cosmetic" constraint, earning its keep). The second kills the
most tempting rescue in advance: "the encoder just needs more epochs" is
refuted by the encoder's own trajectory here — more epochs helped neither
pipeline, and what both actually need is a better-shaped loss and early
stopping, which the literature's tuned numbers (shallow models near 0.34)
spend real search budgets to find. Extrapolation arguments must survive
being measured.

Sit with the discomfort rather than explaining it away,
because each candidate explanation you might reach for is itself
instructive. *"Train the encoder longer"* — the gap at 15
epochs is smaller than at 5, so extrapolation helps the encoder, but the
compute bill scales with it: equal-wall-clock comparisons get worse for
R-GCN, not better. *"Tune it properly"* — the reproduction literature did
(your Week-8 skepticism training pays off here): systematic re-evaluations
find well-tuned *shallow* models at MRR ≈ 0.34 on this benchmark, leading or
matching every GNN encoder, a finding published under the title *"You CAN
Teach an Old Dog New Tricks"* ([Ruffinelli et al., 2020](https://openreview.net/forum?id=BkxSmlBFvr)).

*"The benchmark is unrepresentative"* — closer, and worth making precise
with the week's last definition.

::: {#def-w10-trans .definition name="Transductive vs. inductive completion"}
A completion benchmark is **transductive** when every test entity also
appears in training, so per-entity parameters — a lookup row — exist for
every query; it is **inductive** when test-time entities are new, so a model
must construct their representations from features and neighborhoods alone.
Read the distinction as deciding who is *allowed to compete*: a lookup table
has no row for an unseen entity and forfeits inductive queries outright.
:::

FB15k-237 is transductive: every test entity
was seen in training, so a lookup table can afford a bespoke vector per
entity, and the encoder's structural sharing buys little. Where encoders
demonstrably earn their cost: entities with *features* (a molecule's atoms,
a paper's abstract), inductive settings where test entities are new (a
lookup has no row for a new node — [Week 7's](07-gnn-design.qmd) SAGE
argument, verbatim), sparse entities that must borrow statistical strength
from neighbors, and *entity classification* on typed graphs — R-GCN's actual
home turf, where it beat the field cleanly. The one-sentence verdict to
carry: **a learned encoder is a mechanism for sharing; it pays exactly when
your entities have something to share and rows in a table when they do not.**

It is also worth knowing, mechanically, what the encoder *did* with its 400
seconds, because the anatomy of the cost is next week's entire subject. Each
gradient step scores one 8,192-triple batch — but before it can score
anything, the encoder must produce entity vectors, and producing them means
one full propagation over all 544 thousand directed edges (both-direction
channels of 272 thousand triples), touching all 14,541 entities, whether or
not they appear in the batch. Thirty-four steps per epoch, five epochs:
roughly *one hundred seventy* full-graph propagations — 156 seconds against
the lookup's 7 — to train on what the lookup handled with O(batch)
embedding updates. The lookup's advantage is not
cleverness; it is that its "encoder" is indexing, and indexing is free. Hold
that anatomy: the moment the graph outgrows memory next week, "full
propagation per step" stops being expensive and becomes impossible, and the
repair (sample the neighborhood per batch) is what turns this week's
architectures into deployable systems.

If our verdict bothers you — it should at least itch — the scientific
response is not to re-run with more epochs but to design the experiment
where the encoder's job description actually applies, and you can specify
it right now with course-grade precision. Take FB15k-237, hold out not
random *triples* but random *entities*: strip 5% of entities from training
entirely, then at test time ask for their links given only their
neighborhoods. The lookup table forfeits — it has no row, the exact
transductive failure Week 3 catalogued — while the encoder computes an
embedding for a node it has never seen from typed messages alone. That
inductive split is where R-GCN-style encoders post their wins in the
literature, and constructing it (with the Week-1 discipline about what
leaks across the boundary) is precisely the kind of evaluation design this
course keeps insisting is the real skill.

One more lens on the same data, because it closes a loop opened in Week 4.
Split the test queries by relation category — the TransE paper's own 1-1 /
1-N / N-1 / N-N taxonomy, computed from train-set fan-outs with the paper's
1.5 threshold — and the widget's second view shows MRR 0.313 on N-1 queries
against 0.139 on N-N, with N-N alone comprising 71% of the test set.

The mechanism is the one you proved in Week 4, now wearing benchmark clothes.
An N-1 relation is (nearly) a *function* — many people, one birthplace each
— so a tail query has one defensible answer and geometry can nail it; that
is the 0.313. An N-N relation admits crowds on both sides, and when we ask
for *the* held-out tail among hundreds of genuinely plausible ones, the
model is being graded partly on information the graph does not contain;
that is the 0.139, and it is a property of the *query distribution*, not
of any model — which is exactly why no encoder in our table moved it much.
The "1-to-N crush" you watched squeeze vectors in a 2-D widget six weeks
ago is where most of a real benchmark's difficulty lives, and knowing that
changes how you read every KG leaderboard from now on: ask for the
category breakdown before applauding a headline MRR.

## When types need attention: metapaths, HAN, HGT

R-GCN listens per *relation*. But much of what matters in a typed graph is a
per-*pattern* phenomenon: co-authorship is not any single edge — it is the
composite `author → paper → author`.

::: {#def-w10-metapath .definition name="Metapath"}
A **metapath** is a sequence of node and relation types — a typed walk
recipe, such as author –writes→ paper –writes⁻¹→ author. Its instances
connect node pairs into a derived *metapath neighborhood*, so each recipe
manufactures a different homogeneous graph from the same typed instance.
Read every metapath as a modeling decision: choosing the recipes IS feature
engineering, with everything Week 2 taught about its costs.
:::

{{< include ../assets/d3/w10-metapath.html >}}

**HAN** ([Wang et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.07293), optional
reading) builds directly on this, in two stacked
attention stages whose division of labor you should be able to recite.
Stage one, *node-level* attention: for each metapath $\Phi$ on the menu,
attend GAT-style over $v$'s $\Phi$-neighborhood — within the co-author
lens, which co-authors matter? — producing one embedding of $v$ per
metapath, $z_v^{\Phi}$. Stage two, *semantic* attention: a small learned
scorer weighs the metapaths themselves — for this task, how much is the
co-author lens worth against the venue lens? — and mixes the
$z_v^{\Phi}$'s with softmax weights shared across all nodes. Those
semantic weights are the architecture's best feature and its résumé line:
they are a *readable* answer to "which pattern carried the prediction,"
the kind of artifact a domain expert can audit and argue with. The
architecture is also exactly as good as its menu: a metapath nobody wrote
down is a signal nobody aggregates, and the menu is written by a human
before training begins.

**HGT** ([Hu et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.01332), required
reading) removes the menu.

::: {#def-w10-metarel .definition name="Meta-relation"}
The **meta-relation** of an edge is the triple ⟨source node type, edge type,
target node type⟩ — e.g. ⟨author, writes, paper⟩. HGT indexes *all* of its
attention parameters by this triple, so the same author node uses different
projections when talking to a paper than when talking to an institution.
:::

Attention is parameterized by the meta-relation with type-specific
projections, transformer-style — three learned roles: a *query* (what I
seek), *keys* (what my neighbors offer), *values* (what they send); Week 13
builds this machinery properly, and the three roles are all you need here. A
paper attending to its authors builds queries with the paper-type
projection, keys and values with the author-type projections, and the
attention's core matrix is indexed by the full triple (author, writes,
paper). Multi-hop patterns are not
enumerated; they *emerge* across layers, because a 2-layer HGT composes
typed hops the way any GNN composes hops — our A–P–V–P–A lens is just two
HGT layers' receptive field, discovered rather than declared. Parameters
scale with the number of *types* and not with relation pairs, and the
paper scaled the machine to a 179-million-node academic graph. The trade
against HAN is legibility for coverage: nothing to forget to enumerate,
nothing human-readable to point at afterward.

And then the audit, because this course does not hand out architecture
recommendations without one. The HGB benchmark study
([Lv et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.14936), optional reading,
title: *"Are we really making much progress?"*) re-implemented twelve
heterogeneous GNNs under one protocol and found that a **properly tuned
plain GAT** — types ignored except for a learnable edge-type embedding —
matches or beats most of them, with much of the published gaps traceable to
feature preprocessing and split choices rather than architecture. Their
constructive artifact, Simple-HGN, is worth thirty seconds of respect
precisely for how little it is: GAT, plus a learnable vector per edge type
that participates in the attention score, plus standard training hygiene.
One typed dial — the *minimal* one — captured most of what the elaborate
machinery captured.

The paper is also a syllabus in how to read
architecture claims after this course: check whether the baselines were
tuned with the same care as the proposal (Week 7's noise floor), whether
the splits match across rows (Week 4's filtered-ranking lesson), and
whether preprocessing differs between lines of the same table. The pattern
— elaborate mechanism, modest tuned-baseline gap — is not unique to
heterogeneous GNNs; you saw it in the KG re-evaluations of Week 4, you
will see it again wherever leaderboards live. That does not make types worthless (our own DBLP measurement
says +5 points over no graph at all, and the *edge-type embedding* that
Simple-HGN keeps is precisely the minimal typed dial); it makes the
*elaborateness* of type machinery a claim requiring Week-7-grade evidence.

**Schema decision procedure**, now slowly enough to point at:

- *few relations, features that matter* → R-GCN, or plain GAT with
  edge-type embeddings;
- *a domain expert with strong pattern knowledge and a need to explain
  decisions* → HAN with their metapaths;
- *many types, web scale, no menu-writer available* → HGT;
- *in every case*: run the untyped baseline first, because five points is
  what types bought on DBLP and you should know what they buy on yours.

## The bridge already under your feet

One more reframing, and it may be the most economically consequential slide
of the course. A relational database *is* a heterogeneous graph. Tables are
node types; rows are nodes; every foreign key is a typed edge; a junction
table is an edge type with attributes. The `orders` table pointing into
`customers` and `products` is `customer ←ordered— order —contains→ product`,
and every enterprise on earth runs on data shaped exactly like this. The
whole bridge fits in one dictionary (@tbl-w10-bridge):

| relational concept | heterogeneous-graph concept |
|---|---|
| table | node type |
| row | node |
| foreign key | typed edge |
| junction table | edge type (its attribute columns → edge features) |
| column of shared entities | promoted to a node type |
| free-text or numeric column | node feature |
| timestamp column | temporal constraint on message passing |

: The database–graph bridge: every relational-schema concept has a typed-graph counterpart — the last two rows are the decisions with teeth. {#tbl-w10-bridge}

Work one mapping end to end, because the mechanics have teeth. A hospital
system: `patients(id, demographics…)`, `visits(id, patient_id, ward,
admitted_at)`, `prescriptions(visit_id, drug_id, dose)`, `drugs(id, class)`.
Node types: patient, visit, drug (and possibly ward, promoted from a column
to a type if wards matter relationally). Typed edges: patient —has_visit→
visit from the foreign key; visit —prescribed→ drug through the junction
table, carrying `dose` as an edge attribute.

Now the two decisions that
separate a clean mapping from a leaky one. First, *promotion*: a column
becomes a node type when its values are shared entities you want messages
to flow through (drug class: yes, free-text notes: no — they become
features). Second, *time*: `admitted_at` is not decoration. A model
predicting readmission must only pass messages along edges that existed
before prediction time, or it commits the exact leak Week 1 diagnosed in
random splits and Week 3 caught in walk-based link prediction — the
temporal edition, and the single most common failure in applied relational
deep learning. Week 14 builds the full discipline (RelBench's tasks are
defined by timestamp cutoffs for precisely this reason); this week, just
notice the schema hands you the leak and the cure in the same column.

The consequence of the bridge runs in both directions. Forward: everything
from this lecture applies to the databases where the world's commercial
data actually lives — typed message passing over customers, orders,
products predicts churn and fraud and demand *without the
feature-engineering step* that armies of analysts currently hand-craft
with SQL joins; that is the pitch of relational deep learning, and Week 14
is devoted to it. Backward: your instincts about databases transfer to
this week's models — a metapath is a JOIN path; HAN's semantic attention
is learning which JOINs matter; a projection is a materialized view that
someone forgot could lose information.

And the economics follow the data:
fraud detection at payment networks is typed-pattern detection (card—
merchant—device—IP rings where the *types* of the connecting entities are
the signal); recommendation at retail scale is user–item–session graphs;
academic search ranks author–paper–venue neighborhoods. When someone asks
what heterogeneous GNNs are *for*, the honest answer is mostly not
"knowledge graphs" — our showdown showed lookups holding that fort — it is
"the world's SQL tables, finally read natively."

## The method: designing a typed model without folklore

The week's transferable procedure, five questions asked in order, each with
a cheap measurement attached:

**Does the graph help at all?** Features-only baseline first (our DBLP MLP:
79.0). No typed anything until untyped-anything beats it.

**Do types help?** Untyped GNN on the merged graph versus one typed model.
The gap is your types budget — spend architecture complexity proportionally
to it, and per HGB, expect the honest gap to be smaller than the papers
advertising it.

**Which patterns carry the signal?** Probe with metapaths before buying
attention: compute two or three metapath-adjacency features (Week 2 skills —
they are matrix products) and feed them to a linear model. If
author–paper–author explains the labels, you know *what* the fancy model
must learn — and you have a floor it must beat.

**Encoder or lookup?** Transductive, featureless, every test entity seen in
training → the lookup is a strong, cheap, dignified baseline; treat encoder
gains over it as claims requiring the matched-budget table this lecture just
showed you. Features, new entities at test time, or sparse long-tail
entities → the encoder has a job description.

**What does the parameter bill say?** Count before training: $(2R{+}1)d^2$
against your triples-per-relation histogram. If rare relations get more
parameters than training examples, decompose (basis if relations plausibly
share, blocks if they don't) — or take CompGCN's route and make relations
vectors from the start.

Watch the procedure run on DBLP, because we did run it. Question one:
features-only MLP, 79.0 ± 0.5 — a strong floor; whatever we build must
clear it. Question two: a typed 2-layer network, 84.0 ± 0.7 — the graph is
worth five points, so type machinery has a budget of "five points minus
what untyped would get," modest by construction. Question three: the
signal, probed, is mostly the co-author metapath — which is why two typed
layers (whose receptive field composes exactly A–P–A) capture it without
any attention machinery. Question four does not arise (the task is node
classification with features — encoder territory by definition). Question
five: $R = 4$ at $d = 64$ puts the full bill at $9 \times 4{,}096 \approx
37$k parameters per layer — three orders of magnitude below the
decomposition-discussion threshold, so R-GCN-style full weights (or the
SAGE-per-edge-type equivalent we actually trained) is simply correct, and
anyone proposing HGT here should be asked, kindly, what disease they are
treating. Ten minutes of procedure, and every architecture decision came
out priced instead of fashionable. @tbl-w10-method is the take-away card:

| question | cheap measurement | on DBLP |
|---|---|---|
| does the graph help? | features-only baseline | MLP 79.0 ± 0.5 — the floor |
| do types help? | untyped GNN vs. typed | typed 84.0 ± 0.7; the gap is the types budget |
| which patterns carry it? | metapath-adjacency probe + linear model | co-author metapath carries most of it |
| encoder or lookup? | match the setting to @def-w10-trans | features present → encoder territory |
| what does the bill say? | @eq-w10-bill vs. triples-per-relation | ≈37k/layer — full weights are fine |

: The five-question design procedure, its cheap measurements, and their DBLP answers. {#tbl-w10-method}

A word on tooling before the pitfalls, because Lab 10 will make this
concrete and because ergonomics quietly decide what gets built. PyG
represents a heterogeneous graph as a `HeteroData` object — a dictionary of
node-type feature matrices and a dictionary of edge stores keyed by the
full (source type, relation, target type) triple — and offers two roads to
a typed model. The explicit road, `HeteroConv`, is a dictionary of
per-edge-type layers whose outputs are aggregated per node type; it is
R-GCN's philosophy as an API, every relation's operator visible and
swappable, and it is exactly what our measured DBLP model this week was
built from (a `SAGEConv` per edge type,
summed).

The automatic road, `to_hetero`, takes a homogeneous model you
already trust and *compiles* it into a typed one — duplicating weights per
type triple — which is how you convert last week's architecture into this
week's without rewriting it, and also how you accidentally multiply your
parameter count by the number of edge types without reading a single
warning. Both roads force the inverse-channel and per-type-feature
decisions this lecture keeps flagging; neither makes them for you. The
lesson generalizes past PyG: heterogeneous modeling is one part equations
and two parts data plumbing, and the plumbing is where the silent failures
live — which is precisely why the lab asserts the plumbing, not just the
accuracy.

## Common pitfalls

**Forgetting inverse channels.** An R-GCN over `cites` with no `cites⁻¹`
channel means being cited teaches a paper nothing. PyG's conventions make
this *your* job (double the edge list, offset the types — Lab 10 makes you
do it and asserts you did); several published "R-GCN underperforms"
results are this bug wearing a conclusion.

**Projecting first, modeling second.** Collapsing author–paper–author to a
co-author graph before the GNN throws away multiplicity, mediators, and
mixed paths — then the model gets blamed. If you must project, project as a
*probe* (the method above), never as the input.

**Per-relation averaging vs global averaging.** $c_{v,r}$ normalizes within
each relation. Swap in a single global mean and high-degree relations
recolonize the update — the exact failure typed weights were hired to
prevent, reintroduced by a normalizer.

**Reading transductive wins as encoder wins.** If every test entity has a
training row, a lookup can match you; claim encoder superiority only with
new-entity or feature-dependent evidence. (And the converse: never deploy a
lookup where new entities arrive hourly.)

**Buying HGT for a four-relation schema.** Typed attention with
meta-relation parameterization solves a problem you do not have at $R = 4$;
at that scale it is extra variance with a transformer's appetite. The
parameter widget is calibrated exactly for this conversation with your
future colleagues.

## In this week's lab

[Lab 10](../labs/lab10.qmd) walks the full arc on real data: the P1 hand
update asserted; DBLP loaded as a `HeteroData` object whose typed edge
dictionary you build and whose author classifier you train (asserting the
+measured gap over the feature-only MLP); the inverse-channel construction
for FB15k-237 done explicitly and asserted; and the showdown reproduced —
lookup-DistMult and R-GCN-DistMult under the identical Lab-4 protocol, with
your numbers landing within tolerance of this lecture's table and a claims
paragraph asking what the encoder did and did not buy.

## Required reading

- **Schlichtkrull et al. — Modeling Relational Data with GCNs** (ESWC 2018).
  The update equation, both decompositions, and the encoder–decoder link
  prediction template. Read §2 closely; skim the per-dataset details.
- **Hu, Dong, Wang, Sun — Heterogeneous Graph Transformer** (WWW 2020).
  Meta-relation-parameterized attention; how it avoids hand-designed
  metapaths. Focus on §4 and the architecture figure; skim the scaling
  sections.

Optional: HAN (WWW 2019) for the metapath-attention alternative; the HGB
study (KDD 2021) for the tuned-GAT reality check; CompGCN (ICLR 2020) for
relations-as-vectors unifying this week with Week 4; ULTRA (ICLR 2024) for
where this line is heading — one pretrained model, zero-shot link prediction
on any KG, relations represented by how they interact rather than by a
learned vocabulary.

## Check your understanding

**Q1.** Compute the R-GCN update at $V$ in the toy instance (features and
weights as in the figure; incoming `published_in` from $P_1, P_2$ with
weight $\tfrac12$; $W_0 = 1$).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Only one typed channel reaches $V$: incoming `published_in` from
$\{P_1, P_2\}$ with $c_{V,r} = 2$: $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{1 + 3}{2} = 1$.
Self: $1 \cdot 2 = 2$. Total $h'(V) = \mathbf{3}$. One-channel nodes are
the degenerate case where typed and untyped layers coincide up to the
weight value — worth noticing, because it says *where* types matter: at
nodes whose neighborhoods mix relations.
</details>

**Q2.** A schema has $R = 24$ relations and you plan $d = 200$. Compute the
full per-layer bill and the basis-30 bill, and make the call.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Full: $(2 \cdot 24 + 1) \cdot 200^2 = 49 \times 40{,}000 = 1.96$M. Basis-30:
$30 \cdot 40{,}000 + 48 \cdot 30 + 40{,}000 = 1.24$M — a 1.6× saving, and
$B = 30$ against 48 channels barely decomposes at all. At this scale the
full version is affordable and keeps relations independent; decomposition
is a treatment for a disease you get at hundreds of relations, not dozens.
</details>

**Q3.** Why does the basis decomposition's coefficient vector $a_r$ deserve
to be called a relation embedding, and which Week-4 model does CompGCN's
subtraction composition secretly import?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$a_r \in \mathbb{R}^B$ is a small dense learned vector, one per relation,
that fully determines the relation's behavior (its mixing of shared bases)
— functionally identical to Week 4's relation vectors, relocated into the
encoder. CompGCN's subtraction operator $\phi(h, r) = h - r$ imports
TransE: composing entity and relation by translation, now inside message
passing rather than in the decoder score.
</details>

**Q4.** Your team proposes replacing the production KG-completion lookup
model with an R-GCN encoder "because message passing is more expressive."
Give the two-sentence measured reply.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
On our matched-budget FB15k-237 run the lookup won every comparison (0.179
vs 0.126 MRR at 5 epochs) at 1/22nd the compute — and more epochs helped
neither pipeline — while tuned reproductions
in the literature agree shallow models lead this benchmark — transductive
completion with featureless entities is the lookup's home game.
Expressiveness is Week 9's axis, not a deployment argument; show me new
entities, features, or sparse-entity sharing in our workload and the
encoder gets a job interview.
</details>

**Q5.** For author $a_5$ in the metapath widget's instance, compute the
A–P–A and A–P–V–P–A neighbor sets by hand and explain the asymmetry.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$a_5$ wrote only $p_4$, whose author set is $\{a_5\}$ alone → A–P–A
neighbors: $\varnothing$. Via venues: $p_4 \to$ ICML $\to \{p_3, p_4\} \to$
authors $\{a_4, a_5\}$ → A–P–V–P–A neighbors: $\{a_4\}$. A solo author has
no co-authors but still has venue-mates — different metapaths genuinely
manufacture different graphs, which is why HAN needs its second, semantic
level of attention to arbitrate between them.
</details>

**Q6.** HAN or HGT for: (a) a hospital deploying a model that must justify
each prediction to clinicians, on a schema its own informaticians know
deeply; (b) a web-scale academic graph with dozens of node types and no one
who can enumerate patterns?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
(a) HAN: the informaticians' pattern knowledge becomes the metapath menu,
and semantic-attention weights give clinicians a readable "co-medication
mattered more than shared-ward" answer. (b) HGT: meta-relation
parameterization needs no menu, shares parameters across the type
explosion, and was built (with its sampling machinery) for exactly that
scale. Both answers should come with the HGB caveat: tune the Simple-HGN
baseline first.
</details>

**Q7.** Map this schema to a heterogeneous graph: tables `users(id, …)`,
`items(id, …)`, `purchases(user_id, item_id, timestamp)`,
`reviews(user_id, item_id, stars, text)`. What are the node types, edge
types, and where do `stars` and `timestamp` live?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Node types: user, item (junction tables become *edges*, not nodes — unless
they carry enough attributes to deserve nodehood). Edge types: `purchased`
(user→item, attribute: timestamp) and `reviewed` (user→item, attributes:
stars, text-derived features). Two typed channels between the same node
pair is precisely what R-GCN handles and projections destroy; a model that
merges them cannot learn that a 1-star review and a purchase should move an
embedding in opposite directions.
</details>

**Q8.** Our showdown's N-N queries (71% of the test set) scored MRR 0.139
under every model. Why should the *category* of a query bound your
expectations, independent of architecture?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
An N-N query has many true answers on both sides; filtered evaluation
removes known ones, but the model must still rank *one* held-out tail above
thousands of plausible candidates for a relation that genuinely admits
many — the information to single out the test answer often is not in the
graph at all. That is a ceiling set by the task's uncertainty, not by
model capacity: Week 9 taught architectural ceilings, this table teaches
epistemic ones, and confusing the two wastes GPU-months.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **heterogeneous graph & schema** (@def-w10-hetero) — a graph plus a type
  system; the schema is the data model, the instance its population.
- **metapath** (@def-w10-metapath) — a typed walk recipe; each recipe
  manufactures a different homogeneous graph from the same data.
- **basis decomposition** (@def-w10-basis) — every relation's weight as a
  mixture of $B$ shared bases; the coefficient vector $a_r$ is a relation
  embedding in disguise.
- **meta-relation** (@def-w10-metarel) — the ⟨source type, edge type, target
  type⟩ triple that indexes HGT's attention.
- **transductive vs. inductive completion** (@def-w10-trans) — whether test
  entities were seen in training; decides whether a lookup may even compete.
- **inverse channels** — the flipped edge list with relation types offset by
  $R$; forget it and you build an information diode.
- **per-relation normalization** — $c_{v,r}$ in @eq-w10-rgcn: average within
  each channel, so no relation wins by count alone.
- **encoder–decoder KG completion** (@alg-w10-showdown) — Week 4's decoder
  with a learned encoder in front; pays exactly when entities have something
  to share.
- **block-diagonal decomposition** (@eq-w10-blocks) — the opposite bet to
  bases: independent relations, low-rank interactions.
- **semantic attention** — HAN's second stage: learned, human-readable
  weights over the metapath menu.
:::

## Where this leaves us

The two halves of this course are now one subject. Knowledge graphs got an
encoder; message passing got types; the basis coefficients turned out to be
relation embeddings; and CompGCN closed the loop formally by putting TransE's
translation inside the aggregation. You hand-computed the typed update,
audited the 4.75-million-parameter bill down to 324 thousand, and — most
importantly — ran the honest experiment and let the lookup table keep its
crown in the arena where it happens to be strong, while writing the encoder's
actual job description: features, new entities, shared structure.

Bank the week's transferable skills too, because they outlive any
particular architecture in it: you can now cost a typed model *before*
training it (parameters against triples-per-relation, the audit that
predicts overfitting from a histogram); you can design a matched-budget
comparison whose asymmetries are findings rather than confounds; you can
read a schema — any schema, SQL included — as a graph with decisions
attached about promotion, direction, and time; and you can meet a new
heterogeneous architecture and locate it in two questions: what plays the
role of the per-relation weight, and who writes the menu of patterns.
Those four travel; the model zoo rotates. And when in doubt, this week's
whole spirit compresses to one instruction: before adding type machinery,
measure what types are worth on your task — then spend exactly that much.

Close the loop yourself before you leave — no notes, one minute: the opener
claimed the untyped layer doesn't merely *struggle* to prefer citations
over venues but *cannot*. Reconstruct why, from the collapsed update's
formula. Then reconstruct the showdown verdict — who won, at what compute
ratio, and the one word naming the setting where the verdict flips. If
both come back cleanly, this week is yours; whichever one doesn't is the
section to reread now, while it costs a minute instead of an exam point.

But notice what our showdown quietly assumed: FB15k-237 fits in one GPU's
memory, whole. Every model this week — like every model since Week 6 — saw
the *entire graph* at every step: full-batch forward passes, 272 thousand
edges at once, embeddings for every entity resident at all times. DBLP was
26 thousand nodes; ogbn-arxiv strained but obeyed at 169 thousand. HGT's
authors, meanwhile, were training on **179 million** nodes — and at that
scale, "load the graph and propagate" is not slow; it is *impossible*, by
orders of magnitude, in any memory you will ever be given. The trick that
makes it possible anyway — sample the neighborhood, accept the noise, bound
the variance — is one you already hold from Week 7: GraphSAGE's bargain
([Hamilton et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216)),
which we treated as a curiosity about receptive fields. Next week it becomes
the entire subject: what happens to message passing when the graph is
bigger than the machine — mini-batching over neighborhoods, historical
embeddings, and the engineering that turned GNNs from a paper subject into
infrastructure that serves recommendations to a billion people before
breakfast.
